On March 14, 1964, the FBI wrote up a phone call from the press: Louise Campbell of Science magazine had questions. She was asking about neutron activation analysis, a laboratory method for measuring trace elements, and its use in the Oswald case.

Campbell's call shows the scientific press probing the investigation's laboratory work while the Warren Commission still sat. The memo is a small record of that contact, the Bureau noting a journalist's interest in its science, preserved as filed.

21306-dick-o-the-fens-a-tale-of-the-grea:
Dick Winthorpe, the squire's son, watches his father plan to drain the Lincolnshire fen and reclaim it as farmland. George Manville Fenn sets the tale in the great eastern swamp, where many locals live by the marsh and want it left alone. When digging starts, trouble follows: houses torched, horses and cows maimed, men shot, even murder.

A constable called in takes a dislike to Dick and his friend Tom Tallington. He tries to pin the crimes on them; at times even Dick's father half believes it. Broad Fenland dialect colours the talk. Fenland birds, boats, and weather fill the spaces between the crimes.
21723-songs-of-the-cattle-trail-and-cow-:
John A. Lomax gathered these cowboy songs and poems for a 1919 Macmillan volume, with a foreword by William Lyon Phelps. Lomax had spent years collecting American ballads, backed by a Harvard fellowship for the work. He had already published a well-known book of cowboy songs. Here he turns to the verse men sang and recited on the cattle trail and in cow camps.

The pieces range from trail songs to comic and tender poems by cowboy poets. Lomax prints them as working folklore, the art of men whose lives were spent on horseback. The book helps keep a fading oral world on the page. It remains a rich source for anyone studying the songs of the American West.
21757-the-hot-swamp:
Eight hundred years before Christ, a Phoenician sea captain named Arkal sails from a Greek port in this Ballantyne romance of old Albion. His ship carries one mast, a great square sail, and fifty oars, with a horse's head at the prow. Phoenician traders pushed past the Pillars of Hercules to the Tin Isles and beyond, seeking tin, amber, and gold.

Arkal's voyage toward Britain drives the tale, into seas and lands strange to his crew. Ballantyne sets his seafaring skills to work on the ancient world. The hot swamp of the title waits in the northern mists. It is a bold change of scene for him: his usual sea tale dressed in the oldest clothes of trade.
